name: Cross Validation
explanation: Splits the data into k folds, trains on k−1 of them and tests on the one left out, rotating through every fold. The average score estimates how well the model will do on unseen data.
source: Stone, 'Cross-Validatory Choice and Assessment of Statistical Predictions', JRSS B, 1974

name: Confusion Matrix
explanation: A table of predicted vs actual classes: true positives, false positives, false negatives and true negatives. Most classification metrics are computed from it.
source: Karl Pearson, 'On the Theory of Contingency and Its Relation to Association and Normal Correlation', 1904 (contingency tables; the name 'confusion matrix' came later)

name: Sensitivity (Recall)
explanation: The share of actual positives the model finds: TP / (TP + FN). Medicine calls it sensitivity; information retrieval calls it recall. Its partner, specificity, is the same idea for the negatives.
source: Yerushalmy, 'Statistical Problems in Assessing Methods of Medical Diagnosis', Public Health Reports, 1947

name: Precision
explanation: Of everything the model flagged as positive, the share that really is positive: TP / (TP + FP). High precision means few false alarms.
source: Kent, Berry, Luehrs & Perry, 'Machine Literature Searching VIII', American Documentation, 1955 (early relevance measures in information retrieval)

name: ROC Curve
explanation: Plots the true positive rate against the false positive rate as the classification threshold moves, showing every trade-off a classifier can make. It comes from radar signal detection.
source: Peterson, Birdsall & Fox, 'The Theory of Signal Detectability', IRE Transactions on Information Theory, 1954

name: AUC
explanation: The area under the ROC curve: the probability that the model ranks a random positive above a random negative. 0.5 is chance, 1.0 is perfect.
source: Hanley & McNeil, 'The Meaning and Use of the Area under a Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) Curve', Radiology, 1982

name: Bias–Variance Tradeoff
explanation: Prediction error splits into bias (the model is too simple and underfits) and variance (it is too sensitive to the training data and overfits). Lowering one usually raises the other.
source: Geman, Bienenstock & Doursat, 'Neural Networks and the Bias/Variance Dilemma', Neural Computation, 1992

name: R-squared
explanation: The share of the variance in the target that the model explains. 1 is a perfect fit; 0 is no better than always predicting the mean.
source: Sewall Wright, 'Correlation and Causation', Journal of Agricultural Research, 1921

name: p-value
explanation: The probability of seeing a result at least this extreme if there were really no effect (the null hypothesis). A small p-value suggests the result is unlikely to be pure chance. It is not the probability that the hypothesis is true.
source: Karl Pearson, chi-squared goodness-of-fit paper, Philosophical Magazine, 1900 (first formal P values); popularized by Fisher, 1925

name: Deviance
explanation: A goodness-of-fit measure for models like logistic regression: twice the log-likelihood gap between a perfect (saturated) model and yours. It plays the role the sum of squared residuals plays in linear regression.
source: Nelder & Wedderburn, 'Generalized Linear Models', JRSS A, 1972

name: Entropy
explanation: The average surprise (uncertainty) in a probability distribution. Decision trees use it to choose splits, and it underlies cross-entropy loss.
source: Shannon, 'A Mathematical Theory of Communication', Bell System Technical Journal, 1948

name: Mutual Information
explanation: How much knowing one variable reduces uncertainty about another. Unlike correlation it also catches non-linear relationships, which makes it useful for feature selection.
source: Shannon, 'A Mathematical Theory of Communication', Bell System Technical Journal, 1948

name: Cosine Similarity
explanation: The cosine of the angle between two vectors: 1 is the same direction, 0 is unrelated, −1 is opposite. It ignores length, so it's the standard way to compare documents and embeddings.
source: Salton, Wong & Yang, 'A Vector Space Model for Automatic Indexing', Communications of the ACM, 1975

name: Chain Rule
explanation: The calculus rule for derivatives of nested functions: d/dx f(g(x)) = f′(g(x))·g′(x). Backpropagation is the chain rule applied layer by layer.
source: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, 1676 memoir (first known use of the chain rule)

name: Log-odds (Logit)
explanation: Odds are p / (1 − p). Taking their logarithm maps probabilities from 0–1 onto all real numbers. Logistic regression is a linear model of the log-odds.
source: Berkson, 'Application of the Logistic Function to Bio-Assay', JASA, 1944 (coined 'logit')

name: Odds Ratio
explanation: The odds of an outcome in one group divided by the odds in another. Exponentiating a logistic regression coefficient gives an odds ratio.
source: Cornfield, 'A Method of Estimating Comparative Rates from Clinical Data', Journal of the National Cancer Institute, 1951

name: Maximum Likelihood
explanation: Choose the parameters that make the observed data most probable. Many losses, such as cross-entropy, are negative log-likelihoods in disguise.
source: Fisher, 'On the Mathematical Foundations of Theoretical Statistics', Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A, 1922

name: Tensor
explanation: In ML, an n-dimensional array of numbers (scalar, vector, matrix and beyond) that frameworks can run on GPUs and track gradients through.
source: Ricci & Levi-Civita, 'Méthodes de calcul différentiel absolu et leurs applications', Mathematische Annalen, 1900 (tensor calculus; ML uses the word more loosely)

name: Least Squares
explanation: Fit a model by minimizing the sum of squared differences between its predictions and the data. Legendre published it first; Gauss said he had used it years earlier.
source: Legendre, 'Nouvelles méthodes pour la détermination des orbites des comètes', 1805

name: Linear Regression
explanation: Fits a straight line (y = intercept + slope·x) through the data, usually by least squares, to predict a number.
source: Galton, 'Regression towards Mediocrity in Hereditary Stature', Journal of the Anthropological Institute, 1886 (named 'regression')

name: Multiple Regression
explanation: Linear regression with several input variables at once. Each coefficient shows one variable's effect while the others are held fixed.
source: Yule, 'On the Theory of Correlation', Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, 1897

name: t-test
explanation: Tests whether two group means differ by more than chance would explain. Gosset published it under the pen name 'Student' while working at the Guinness brewery.
source: 'Student' (W. S. Gosset), 'The Probable Error of a Mean', Biometrika, 1908

name: ANOVA
explanation: Tests whether the means of three or more groups differ, by comparing the variance between groups with the variance within them.
source: Fisher, 'Statistical Methods for Research Workers', 1925

name: Logistic Regression
explanation: Predicts the probability of a yes/no outcome by passing a weighted sum of the inputs through the S-shaped logistic (sigmoid) function. Fitted with maximum likelihood.
source: Cox, 'The Regression Analysis of Binary Sequences', JRSS B, 1958

name: Ridge Regression
explanation: Linear regression plus a penalty on the squared size of the coefficients (L2). It shrinks them toward zero, which lowers variance and helps when inputs are correlated.
source: Hoerl & Kennard, 'Ridge Regression: Biased Estimation for Nonorthogonal Problems', Technometrics, 1970

name: Lasso Regression
explanation: Linear regression with a penalty on the absolute size of the coefficients (L1). It can push coefficients exactly to zero, so it also selects features.
source: Tibshirani, 'Regression Shrinkage and Selection via the Lasso', JRSS B, 1996

name: Elastic Net
explanation: Combines the Ridge (L2) and Lasso (L1) penalties: it keeps Lasso's feature selection while handling groups of correlated features better.
source: Zou & Hastie, 'Regularization and Variable Selection via the Elastic Net', JRSS B, 2005

name: Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
explanation: Rotates the data onto new axes (principal components) ordered by how much variance each captures, so you can keep the first few and drop the rest.
source: Pearson, 'On Lines and Planes of Closest Fit to Systems of Points in Space', Philosophical Magazine, 1901 (named by Hotelling, 1933)

name: Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA)
explanation: Finds the axes that best separate known classes, maximizing the spread between classes relative to the spread within them. Like PCA, but it uses the labels.
source: Fisher, 'The Use of Multiple Measurements in Taxonomic Problems', Annals of Eugenics, 1936

name: Multidimensional Scaling (MDS)
explanation: Places points in 2-D or 3-D so that their distances match a given distance matrix as closely as possible. With Euclidean distances, classical MDS (PCoA) gives the same picture as PCA.
source: Torgerson, 'Multidimensional Scaling: I. Theory and Method', Psychometrika, 1952 (PCoA: Gower, 1966)

name: t-SNE
explanation: Squeezes high-dimensional data into 2-D for plotting by keeping similar points close together. Great for spotting clusters, but the distances between clusters don't mean much.
source: van der Maaten & Hinton, 'Visualizing Data using t-SNE', JMLR, 2008

name: Hierarchical Clustering
explanation: Starts with every point as its own cluster and repeatedly merges the two closest ones, drawing the history as a tree (dendrogram) you can cut at any level.
source: Ward, 'Hierarchical Grouping to Optimize an Objective Function', JASA, 1963

name: K-means
explanation: Splits the data into k clusters by alternating two steps: assign each point to its nearest centre, then move each centre to the mean of its points.
source: MacQueen, 'Some Methods for Classification and Analysis of Multivariate Observations', 5th Berkeley Symposium, 1967 (same algorithm: Lloyd, 1957, published 1982)

name: DBSCAN
explanation: Grows clusters out of dense regions and labels isolated points as noise. It finds clusters of any shape and doesn't need the number of clusters up front.
source: Ester, Kriegel, Sander & Xu, 'A Density-Based Algorithm for Discovering Clusters in Large Spatial Databases with Noise', KDD, 1996

name: K-Nearest Neighbors
explanation: Predicts for a new point by a vote (or average) of the k closest training points. There's no training step: it just memorizes the data.
source: Fix & Hodges, 'Discriminatory Analysis. Nonparametric Discrimination', USAF School of Aviation Medicine report, 1951 (analysed by Cover & Hart, 1967)

name: Naive Bayes
explanation: Applies Bayes' theorem with the 'naive' assumption that features are independent given the class. Fast and surprisingly good: a classic spam filter.
source: Maron, 'Automatic Indexing: An Experimental Inquiry', Journal of the ACM, 1961

name: Decision Tree
explanation: A flowchart of yes/no questions about the features, learned by repeatedly picking the split that makes the groups purest (for example, lowest Gini impurity).
source: Breiman, Friedman, Olshen & Stone, 'Classification and Regression Trees', 1984 (earlier trees: Morgan & Sonquist, 1963; ID3: Quinlan, 1986)

name: Regression Tree
explanation: A decision tree that predicts numbers: each leaf outputs the average target of the training examples that end up there.
source: Breiman, Friedman, Olshen & Stone, 'Classification and Regression Trees', 1984

name: Tree Pruning
explanation: Cuts back the branches of a fully grown tree, giving up a little training accuracy for a simpler tree that overfits less. Cost-complexity pruning picks how much to cut using cross validation.
source: Breiman, Friedman, Olshen & Stone, 'Classification and Regression Trees', 1984

name: Random Forest
explanation: Many decision trees, each trained on a bootstrap sample and a random subset of features at every split, voting together. Far less overfitting than a single tree.
source: Breiman, 'Random Forests', Machine Learning, 2001

name: Support Vector Machine
explanation: Finds the boundary with the widest margin between the classes; only the closest points (the support vectors) decide where it goes. With kernels it can draw curved boundaries.
source: Cortes & Vapnik, 'Support-Vector Networks', Machine Learning, 1995

name: Kernel Trick
explanation: Computes dot products as if the data had been mapped into a higher-dimensional space, without ever building that space. It lets SVMs learn curved boundaries; polynomial and RBF are the common kernels.
source: Boser, Guyon & Vapnik, 'A Training Algorithm for Optimal Margin Classifiers', COLT, 1992

name: Target Encoding
explanation: Replaces each category with the average target value for that category. Powerful for features with many categories, but it needs care (such as k-fold encoding) to avoid leaking the target.
source: Micci-Barreca, 'A Preprocessing Scheme for High-Cardinality Categorical Attributes in Classification and Prediction Problems', SIGKDD Explorations, 2001

name: Gradient Descent
explanation: Minimizes a loss by repeatedly nudging the parameters in the direction that lowers it fastest (the negative gradient). The learning rate sets the step size.
source: Cauchy, 'Méthode générale pour la résolution des systèmes d'équations simultanées', Comptes Rendus, 1847

name: Stochastic Gradient Descent
explanation: Gradient descent that estimates the gradient from a random sample (or mini-batch) instead of the whole dataset. The steps are noisier but far cheaper, which is how large neural networks are trained.
source: Robbins & Monro, 'A Stochastic Approximation Method', Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 1951

name: Backpropagation
explanation: Computes the gradient of the loss for every weight in a neural network by applying the chain rule backwards from the output, one layer at a time.
source: Rumelhart, Hinton & Williams, 'Learning Representations by Back-Propagating Errors', Nature, 1986 (earlier: Linnainmaa, 1970; Werbos, 1974)

name: AdaBoost
explanation: Builds a sequence of tiny trees (stumps), each focusing on the examples the previous ones got wrong, and combines them in a weighted vote.
source: Freund & Schapire, 'A Decision-Theoretic Generalization of On-Line Learning and an Application to Boosting', Journal of Computer and System Sciences, 1997 (conference version 1995)

name: Gradient Boosting
explanation: Adds trees one at a time, each fitted to the residuals (the gradient of the loss) of the model so far and scaled by a learning rate.
source: Friedman, 'Greedy Function Approximation: A Gradient Boosting Machine', Annals of Statistics, 2001

name: XGBoost
explanation: A fast, regularized gradient boosting system with clever engineering (similarity scores, sparsity-aware splits, cache-aware computation). For years it dominated tabular-data competitions.
source: Chen & Guestrin, 'XGBoost: A Scalable Tree Boosting System', KDD, 2016

name: CatBoost
explanation: Yandex's gradient boosting library. It handles categorical features with ordered target encoding and uses symmetric trees, which reduce target leakage and overfitting.
source: Prokhorenkova et al., 'CatBoost: Unbiased Boosting with Categorical Features', NeurIPS, 2018 (Yandex)

name: Neural Network
explanation: Layers of simple units, each taking a weighted sum of its inputs and passing it through an activation function. Stacked and trained by backpropagation, they can fit almost any function.
source: McCulloch & Pitts, 'A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity', Bulletin of Mathematical Biophysics, 1943

name: ReLU
explanation: The activation function max(0, x): positives pass through, negatives become zero. It's cheap and keeps gradients healthy, so it became the default in deep networks.
source: Nair & Hinton, 'Rectified Linear Units Improve Restricted Boltzmann Machines', ICML, 2010

name: Softmax
explanation: Turns a vector of raw scores into probabilities that are positive and sum to 1, by exponentiating each score and dividing by the total. ArgMax just picks the biggest score.
source: Bridle, 'Probabilistic Interpretation of Feedforward Classification Network Outputs, with Relationships to Statistical Pattern Recognition', 1990 (named 'softmax')

name: Cross Entropy
explanation: The standard loss for classification: −log of the probability the model gave to the correct class. Confident wrong answers are punished hard.
source: I. J. Good, 'Rational Decisions', JRSS B, 1952 (logarithmic scoring rule, i.e. log loss; builds on Shannon's entropy, 1948)

name: Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)
explanation: A network that slides small learned filters across an image, so the same pattern detector works everywhere. Pooling layers shrink the image as the features get more abstract.
source: LeCun et al., 'Backpropagation Applied to Handwritten Zip Code Recognition', Neural Computation, 1989 (inspired by Fukushima's Neocognitron, 1980)

name: Recurrent Neural Network (RNN)
explanation: Processes a sequence one step at a time, feeding its hidden state back in, so earlier inputs affect later outputs. On long sequences its gradients vanish or explode.
source: Elman, 'Finding Structure in Time', Cognitive Science, 1990 (earlier: Jordan, 1986)

name: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)
explanation: An RNN with a separate long-term memory and gates that decide what to forget, store and output, so it can learn dependencies across long sequences.
source: Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 'Long Short-Term Memory', Neural Computation, 1997

name: Word2Vec
explanation: Learns a vector for each word by predicting words from their neighbours (or the reverse), so words used in similar contexts end up close together: king − man + woman ≈ queen.
source: Mikolov, Chen, Corrado & Dean, 'Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space', 2013 (Google)

name: Seq2seq (Encoder–Decoder)
explanation: An encoder network reads the input sequence into a context vector, and a decoder network generates the output sequence from it. It was built for machine translation.
source: Sutskever, Vinyals & Le, 'Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks', NeurIPS, 2014 (Google; see also Cho et al., 2014)

name: Attention
explanation: Lets a model look back at every input position and weight each one by how relevant it is to the current step, instead of squeezing everything into one fixed vector.
source: Bahdanau, Cho & Bengio, 'Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate', 2014 (ICLR 2015)

name: Transformer
explanation: Drops recurrence and relies on self-attention plus positional encodings, so whole sequences are processed in parallel. It's the architecture behind modern LLMs.
source: Vaswani et al., 'Attention Is All You Need', NeurIPS, 2017 (Google)

name: Decoder-only Transformer (GPT)
explanation: Keeps only the transformer's decoder with masked self-attention, so each token sees only earlier ones. Trained to predict the next token, it's the design behind ChatGPT-style models.
source: Radford, Narasimhan, Salimans & Sutskever, 'Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training', OpenAI, 2018

name: BERT (Encoder-only Transformer)
explanation: Keeps only the transformer's encoder and lets every token attend in both directions. Pre-trained by filling in masked words, it's used for classification, search and embeddings (for example in RAG).
source: Devlin, Chang, Lee & Toutanova, 'BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding', 2018 (Google; NAACL 2019)

name: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
explanation: Before answering, retrieve relevant documents (often by embedding similarity) and add them to the model's input, so answers can draw on fresh or private knowledge.
source: Lewis et al., 'Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks', NeurIPS, 2020 (Facebook AI Research)

name: PyTorch
explanation: Meta's open-source deep learning library: GPU tensors, automatic differentiation and a Python-first style. Lightning adds structure on top for training loops.
source: First public release by Facebook AI Research, 2016; paper: Paszke et al., 'PyTorch: An Imperative Style, High-Performance Deep Learning Library', NeurIPS, 2019

name: Dropout
explanation: Randomly switches off a fraction of neurons at each training step, so the network can't rely on any single one. A simple, strong defence against overfitting.
source: Srivastava, Hinton, Krizhevsky, Sutskever & Salakhutdinov, 'Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting', JMLR, 2014

name: Batch Normalization
explanation: Rescales each layer's activations to zero mean and unit variance across the mini-batch, then applies a learned scale and shift. Makes deep networks train faster and more stably.
source: Ioffe & Szegedy, 'Batch Normalization: Accelerating Deep Network Training by Reducing Internal Covariate Shift', ICML, 2015 (Google)

name: Layer Normalization
explanation: Normalizes across the features of each single example instead of across the batch, so it works with any batch size. It's the normalization used inside transformers.
source: Ba, Kiros & Hinton, 'Layer Normalization', arXiv, 2016

name: Adam
explanation: Gradient descent with momentum plus a per-parameter step size that adapts to how large that parameter's gradients have been. The default optimizer for most deep learning.
source: Kingma & Ba, 'Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization', arXiv 2014 (ICLR 2015)

name: Momentum
explanation: Lets gradient descent build up speed: each step adds a fraction of the previous step, which smooths out zig-zags and rolls through small bumps in the loss.
source: Polyak, 'Some Methods of Speeding Up the Convergence of Iteration Methods', USSR Computational Mathematics and Mathematical Physics, 1964

name: Sigmoid
explanation: The S-shaped function 1 / (1 + e^(−x)) that squashes any number into 0–1. It turns scores into probabilities in logistic regression and was the classic neural activation.
source: Verhulst, 'Notice sur la loi que la population suit dans son accroissement', 1838 (named 'logistique' in 1845)

name: Generative Adversarial Network (GAN)
explanation: Two networks trained against each other: a generator makes fakes and a discriminator tries to spot them. As both improve, the generator learns to produce realistic data.
source: Goodfellow et al., 'Generative Adversarial Nets', NeurIPS, 2014

name: Autoencoder
explanation: A network trained to reproduce its input through a narrow bottleneck, so the bottleneck learns a compact code for the data. Used for compression, denoising and anomaly detection.
source: Hinton & Salakhutdinov, 'Reducing the Dimensionality of Data with Neural Networks', Science, 2006 (the idea dates back to the 1980s)

name: Variational Autoencoder (VAE)
explanation: An autoencoder whose code is a probability distribution, trained with the reparameterization trick. Sampling from that distribution and decoding generates new data.
source: Kingma & Welling, 'Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes', arXiv 2013 (ICLR 2014)

name: Diffusion Model
explanation: Learns to reverse a process that gradually adds noise to data. To generate, start from pure noise and denoise step by step: the idea behind Stable Diffusion and DALL·E 2.
source: Sohl-Dickstein, Weiss, Maheswaranathan & Ganguli, 'Deep Unsupervised Learning using Nonequilibrium Thermodynamics', ICML, 2015 (made practical by Ho, Jain & Abbeel, DDPM, 2020)

name: ResNet
explanation: A very deep CNN where each block adds its input back to its output (a skip connection). Gradients flow through the shortcuts, which made networks with 100+ layers trainable.
source: He, Zhang, Ren & Sun, 'Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition', arXiv 2015 (CVPR 2016; Microsoft Research)

name: AlexNet
explanation: The CNN that won ImageNet 2012 by a huge margin, trained on GPUs with ReLU and dropout. It kicked off the deep learning boom.
source: Krizhevsky, Sutskever & Hinton, 'ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks', NeurIPS, 2012

name: Perceptron
explanation: A single artificial neuron that learns a linear boundary by nudging its weights after each mistake. It can't learn XOR, a limit that later multi-layer networks overcame.
source: Rosenblatt, 'The Perceptron: A Probabilistic Model for Information Storage and Organization in the Brain', Psychological Review, 1958

name: Vanishing Gradient
explanation: In deep or recurrent networks, gradients multiply through many layers and can shrink to nearly zero (or blow up), so early layers stop learning. ReLU, LSTM and skip connections all help.
source: Hochreiter, 'Untersuchungen zu dynamischen neuronalen Netzen', diploma thesis, TU Munich, 1991 (also Bengio, Simard & Frasconi, 1994)

name: Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
explanation: Builds a vocabulary of subword tokens by repeatedly merging the most frequent pair of symbols. Most LLM tokenizers use it, so rare words split into common pieces.
source: Sennrich, Haddow & Birch, 'Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units', ACL, 2016 (compression algorithm: Gage, 1994)

name: LoRA
explanation: Fine-tunes a big model by freezing its weights and training small low-rank matrices added beside them. A tiny fraction of the parameters, with results close to full fine-tuning.
source: Hu et al., 'LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models', arXiv 2021 (ICLR 2022; Microsoft)

name: RLHF
explanation: Train a reward model on human preferences between outputs, then fine-tune the policy (for example an LLM) with reinforcement learning to score well on it. How chatbots are taught to be helpful.
source: Christiano et al., 'Deep Reinforcement Learning from Human Preferences', NeurIPS, 2017 (OpenAI & DeepMind); applied to LLMs in InstructGPT, Ouyang et al., 2022

name: Q-learning
explanation: Learns the value Q(state, action) of every action from trial and error, updating each estimate toward reward + the best next value. Then act by picking the highest Q.
source: Watkins, 'Learning from Delayed Rewards', PhD thesis, University of Cambridge, 1989

name: Deep Q-Network (DQN)
explanation: Q-learning with a neural network estimating the Q-values, stabilized by experience replay and a target network. It learned to play Atari games from raw pixels.
source: Mnih et al., 'Playing Atari with Deep Reinforcement Learning', arXiv, 2013 (DeepMind; Nature version 2015)

name: Markov Decision Process (MDP)
explanation: The maths of sequential decisions: states, actions, transition probabilities and rewards. Reinforcement learning is about finding a good policy in an MDP.
source: Bellman, 'A Markovian Decision Process', Journal of Mathematics and Mechanics, 1957

name: Policy Gradient
explanation: Trains a policy directly: make the actions that led to high reward more likely by following the gradient of expected reward. The basis of RL with neural networks, including RLHF.
source: Williams, 'Simple Statistical Gradient-Following Algorithms for Connectionist Reinforcement Learning', Machine Learning, 1992 (REINFORCE)

name: Multi-armed Bandit
explanation: Choose repeatedly between slot machines with unknown payouts. The core trade-off of reinforcement learning: exploit what seems best or explore to learn more.
source: Robbins, 'Some Aspects of the Sequential Design of Experiments', Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society, 1952 (related: Thompson, 1933)

name: Bayes' Theorem
explanation: P(A|B) = P(B|A)·P(A) / P(B): how to update a belief after seeing evidence. The basis of Naive Bayes and all of Bayesian statistics.
source: Bayes, 'An Essay towards Solving a Problem in the Doctrine of Chances', Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society, 1763 (published posthumously by Price)

name: Normal Distribution
explanation: The bell curve, defined by its mean and standard deviation. Many measurements are roughly normal, and lots of models (linear regression, Gaussian Naive Bayes) assume it.
source: Gauss, 'Theoria motus corporum coelestium', 1809 (earlier form: de Moivre, 1733)

name: Central Limit Theorem
explanation: Averages of many independent samples are approximately normally distributed, whatever the original distribution. It's why t-tests and confidence intervals work.
source: Laplace, memoir to the Paris Academy of Sciences, 1810 (special case: de Moivre, 1733)

name: Bootstrapping
explanation: Estimate how uncertain a statistic is by resampling the data with replacement many times and recomputing it each time. Random forests use bootstrap samples too.
source: Efron, 'Bootstrap Methods: Another Look at the Jackknife', Annals of Statistics, 1979

name: Bagging
explanation: Train many copies of a model on different bootstrap samples and average (or vote on) their predictions. Cuts variance; random forests are bagged trees plus feature sampling.
source: Breiman, 'Bagging Predictors', Machine Learning, 1996

name: Gini Impurity
explanation: The chance of mislabelling a random item if you labelled it at random according to the class mix of its group: 1 − Σ p². Decision trees pick the split with the lowest impurity.
source: Gini, 'Variabilità e mutabilità', 1912 (used for tree splits in CART, Breiman et al., 1984)

name: F1 Score
explanation: The harmonic mean of precision and recall, so it's only high when both are. A common single score for imbalanced classes.
source: van Rijsbergen, 'Information Retrieval', 2nd edition, 1979 (the F-measure)

name: Pearson Correlation
explanation: A number from −1 to 1 measuring how well two variables follow a straight-line relationship. It misses non-linear patterns, and correlation isn't causation.
source: Karl Pearson, 'Note on Regression and Inheritance in the Case of Two Parents', Proceedings of the Royal Society of London, 1895 (idea from Galton, 1888)

name: SMOTE
explanation: Balances an imbalanced dataset by creating synthetic minority-class examples along the lines between existing ones and their nearest neighbours.
source: Chawla, Bowyer, Hall & Kegelmeyer, 'SMOTE: Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique', JAIR, 2002

name: Expectation–Maximization (EM)
explanation: Fits models with hidden variables by alternating two steps: guess the hidden parts given the parameters (E), then refit the parameters given those guesses (M). Used for Gaussian mixtures.
source: Dempster, Laird & Rubin, 'Maximum Likelihood from Incomplete Data via the EM Algorithm', JRSS B, 1977

name: Hidden Markov Model (HMM)
explanation: A sequence of hidden states that follow a Markov chain, each emitting an observation. Before deep learning it powered speech recognition and part-of-speech tagging.
source: Baum & Petrie, 'Statistical Inference for Probabilistic Functions of Finite State Markov Chains', Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 1966

name: Markov Chain
explanation: A random process where the next state depends only on the current one, not on the history. The building block of HMMs, MDPs and MCMC.
source: Andrey Markov, paper on the law of large numbers for dependent variables, Izvestiya of the Physico-Mathematical Society of Kazan University, 1906

name: Singular Value Decomposition (SVD)
explanation: Factors any matrix into rotation × scaling × rotation (UΣVᵀ). Keeping the largest singular values gives the best low-rank approximation; PCA is usually computed this way.
source: Beltrami, 1873, and independently Jordan, 1874 (best low-rank approximation: Eckart & Young, 1936)

name: UMAP
explanation: Like t-SNE, it maps high-dimensional data to 2-D by keeping neighbours close, but it's faster and tends to keep more of the global structure.
source: McInnes, Healy & Melville, 'UMAP: Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection for Dimension Reduction', arXiv, 2018

name: LightGBM
explanation: Microsoft's gradient boosting library. It grows trees leaf-wise and uses histogram-based splits with gradient-based sampling, which makes it very fast on big tabular data.
source: Ke et al., 'LightGBM: A Highly Efficient Gradient Boosting Decision Tree', NeurIPS, 2017 (Microsoft)

name: scikit-learn
explanation: The standard Python library for classical ML: the same fit / predict interface for regression, trees, SVMs, clustering, PCA, cross validation and more.
source: First public release 2010 (project started 2007); paper: Pedregosa et al., 'Scikit-learn: Machine Learning in Python', JMLR, 2011

name: TensorFlow
explanation: Google's open-source deep learning framework, built around tensors flowing through a computation graph. Keras became its high-level API.
source: Open-sourced by Google Brain, November 2015; Abadi et al., 'TensorFlow: A System for Large-Scale Machine Learning', OSDI, 2016

name: NumPy
explanation: Python's fast n-dimensional array library. Almost every Python ML tool, from pandas to scikit-learn, is built on it.
source: NumPy 1.0 released by Travis Oliphant, 2006; Harris et al., 'Array Programming with NumPy', Nature, 2020

name: GloVe
explanation: Word vectors learned from global word co-occurrence counts, so that dot products of vectors match how often words appear together. Stanford's alternative to Word2Vec.
source: Pennington, Socher & Manning, 'GloVe: Global Vectors for Word Representation', EMNLP, 2014

name: Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU)
explanation: A simpler LSTM with two gates (update and reset) and no separate memory cell. It often matches LSTM accuracy with fewer parameters.
source: Cho et al., 'Learning Phrase Representations using RNN Encoder–Decoder for Statistical Machine Translation', EMNLP, 2014

name: Positional Encoding
explanation: Attention itself ignores word order, so transformers add a position signal (originally sine and cosine waves of different frequencies) to each token's embedding.
source: Vaswani et al., 'Attention Is All You Need', NeurIPS, 2017 (Google)

name: Vision Transformer (ViT)
explanation: Cuts an image into 16×16 patches and feeds them to a standard transformer as if they were words. With enough data it beats CNNs.
source: Dosovitskiy et al., 'An Image is Worth 16x16 Words: Transformers for Image Recognition at Scale', arXiv 2020 (ICLR 2021; Google)

name: CLIP
explanation: Trains an image encoder and a text encoder together so matching image–caption pairs land close in the same embedding space. It can classify images from text labels it never trained on.
source: Radford et al., 'Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision', ICML, 2021 (OpenAI)

name: Mixture of Experts (MoE)
explanation: Several expert sub-networks plus a gating network that decides which experts handle each input. Modern LLMs use sparse MoE to grow parameters without growing compute per token.
source: Jacobs, Jordan, Nowlan & Hinton, 'Adaptive Mixtures of Local Experts', Neural Computation, 1991 (sparse MoE for LLMs: Shazeer et al., 2017)

name: Chain-of-Thought Prompting
explanation: Get an LLM to write out intermediate reasoning steps before the final answer. It greatly improves results on maths and multi-step problems.
source: Wei et al., 'Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models', NeurIPS, 2022 (Google)

name: In-context Learning
explanation: An LLM picks up a new task from examples or instructions in its prompt, with no weight updates at all.
source: Brown et al., 'Language Models are Few-Shot Learners', NeurIPS, 2020 (OpenAI, GPT-3)

name: Knowledge Distillation
explanation: Train a small 'student' model to match the soft output probabilities of a big 'teacher', squeezing most of the teacher's skill into a cheaper model.
source: Hinton, Vinyals & Dean, 'Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network', arXiv, 2015 (Google)

name: Perplexity
explanation: How 'surprised' a language model is by real text: the exponential of the average cross-entropy per token. Lower is better; roughly the number of words it's choosing between.
source: Jelinek, Mercer, Bahl & Baker, 'Perplexity: A Measure of the Difficulty of Speech Recognition Tasks', Journal of the Acoustical Society of America, 1977 (IBM)

name: BLEU Score
explanation: Scores machine translation by how many word n-grams it shares with human reference translations, with a penalty for being too short.
source: Papineni, Roukos, Ward & Zhu, 'BLEU: a Method for Automatic Evaluation of Machine Translation', ACL, 2002 (IBM)

name: Xavier Initialization
explanation: Sets the starting weights' scale from the layer's fan-in and fan-out, so signals keep roughly the same variance through the layers. He initialization adapts it for ReLU.
source: Glorot & Bengio, 'Understanding the Difficulty of Training Deep Feedforward Neural Networks', AISTATS, 2010

name: Mahalanobis Distance
explanation: Distance from a point to a distribution that accounts for correlations and scale: it's Euclidean distance after 'whitening' the data. Useful for outlier detection.
source: Mahalanobis, 'On the Generalised Distance in Statistics', Proceedings of the National Institute of Sciences of India, 1936

name: Silhouette Score
explanation: For each point, compares the distance to its own cluster with the distance to the nearest other cluster (−1 to 1). Used to judge clusterings and to pick k.
source: Rousseeuw, 'Silhouettes: A Graphical Aid to the Interpretation and Validation of Cluster Analysis', Journal of Computational and Applied Mathematics, 1987

name: ARIMA
explanation: Forecasts a time series from its own past values (AR) and past errors (MA), after differencing to remove trends (I). The classic statistical forecasting model.
source: Box & Jenkins, 'Time Series Analysis: Forecasting and Control', 1970

name: KL Divergence
explanation: How different one probability distribution is from another: the extra bits needed if you code samples from P using a code built for Q. Not symmetric. Appears in VAEs and RLHF.
source: Kullback & Leibler, 'On Information and Sufficiency', Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 1951

name: Monte Carlo Method
explanation: Estimate a quantity that's hard to compute exactly by averaging over many random samples. Named after the Monaco casino.
source: Metropolis & Ulam, 'The Monte Carlo Method', JASA, 1949

name: Scaling Laws
explanation: A language model's loss falls as a smooth power law as you scale up parameters, data and compute. That's why labs kept building bigger models.
source: Kaplan et al., 'Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models', arXiv, 2020 (OpenAI)

name: Self-Organizing Map
explanation: A grid of neurons that learns to arrange itself over the data, so similar inputs map to nearby grid cells. A neural way to cluster and visualize.
source: Kohonen, 'Self-Organized Formation of Topologically Correct Feature Maps', Biological Cybernetics, 1982

name: Universal Approximation Theorem
explanation: A neural network with one hidden layer and enough neurons can approximate any continuous function as closely as you like. It says nothing about how to find the weights.
source: Cybenko, 'Approximation by Superpositions of a Sigmoidal Function', Mathematics of Control, Signals and Systems, 1989

name: Curse of Dimensionality
explanation: As the number of features grows, space gets so empty that data becomes sparse and distances lose meaning. Methods like KNN suffer most.
source: Bellman, 'Dynamic Programming', Princeton University Press, 1957

name: SHAP
explanation: Explains a single prediction by sharing it out among the features using Shapley values from game theory: each feature's fair contribution to the result.
source: Lundberg & Lee, 'A Unified Approach to Interpreting Model Predictions', NeurIPS, 2017

name: LIME
explanation: Explains one prediction of any black-box model by fitting a simple model (such as a linear one) to its behaviour on small perturbations around that input.
source: Ribeiro, Singh & Guestrin, "'Why Should I Trust You?': Explaining the Predictions of Any Classifier", KDD, 2016

name: YOLO
explanation: Detects objects in one pass: a single CNN looks at the whole image once and directly regresses bounding boxes and class probabilities on a grid. Fast enough for real-time video.
source: Redmon, Divvala, Girshick & Farhadi, 'You Only Look Once: Unified, Real-Time Object Detection', arXiv 2015 (CVPR 2016)

name: U-Net
explanation: A U-shaped CNN for segmentation: an encoder shrinks the image, a decoder grows it back, and skip connections pass fine details across, so it labels every pixel. Also the backbone of many diffusion models.
source: Ronneberger, Fischer & Brox, 'U-Net: Convolutional Networks for Biomedical Image Segmentation', MICCAI, 2015

name: Faster R-CNN
explanation: A two-stage object detector: a region proposal network suggests boxes that might contain objects, then a second head classifies and refines each one.
source: Ren, He, Girshick & Sun, 'Faster R-CNN: Towards Real-Time Object Detection with Region Proposal Networks', NeurIPS, 2015 (Microsoft Research)

name: VGG
explanation: A very deep CNN built only from small 3×3 convolutions stacked 16–19 layers deep. Showed that depth matters, and its features were reused everywhere.
source: Simonyan & Zisserman, 'Very Deep Convolutional Networks for Large-Scale Image Recognition', arXiv 2014 (ICLR 2015; Oxford)

name: Inception (GoogLeNet)
explanation: A CNN whose blocks run 1×1, 3×3 and 5×5 convolutions side by side and concatenate them, using 1×1 convolutions to keep it cheap. Won ImageNet 2014.
source: Szegedy et al., 'Going Deeper with Convolutions', arXiv 2014 (CVPR 2015; Google)

name: LeNet
explanation: One of the first successful CNNs: convolution, pooling and fully connected layers that read handwritten digits on bank cheques.
source: LeCun, Bottou, Bengio & Haffner, 'Gradient-Based Learning Applied to Document Recognition', Proceedings of the IEEE, 1998

name: Transfer Learning
explanation: Reuse a model trained on one task as the starting point for another, then fine-tune it on the new data. Why you rarely train big models from scratch.
source: Pratt, 'Discriminability-Based Transfer between Neural Networks', NeurIPS, 1993 (an early formal treatment; the idea has several origins)

name: MNIST
explanation: 70,000 small grayscale images of handwritten digits 0–9. The 'hello world' of image classification.
source: LeCun, Cortes & Burges, MNIST database, 1998 (built from NIST data; used in LeCun et al., Proceedings of the IEEE, 1998)

name: ImageNet
explanation: Over 14 million labelled images in more than 20,000 categories. Its yearly challenge (ILSVRC) is where AlexNet started the deep learning boom in 2012.
source: Deng, Dong, Socher, Li, Li & Fei-Fei, 'ImageNet: A Large-Scale Hierarchical Image Database', CVPR, 2009

name: Iris Dataset
explanation: 150 iris flowers, 4 measurements each, 3 species. The classic first dataset for classification and clustering.
source: Fisher, 'The Use of Multiple Measurements in Taxonomic Problems', Annals of Eugenics, 1936 (data collected by Edgar Anderson)

name: COCO Dataset
explanation: Over 300,000 everyday-scene images with object boxes, segmentation masks and captions. The standard benchmark for object detection.
source: Lin et al., 'Microsoft COCO: Common Objects in Context', ECCV, 2014 (Microsoft)

name: TF-IDF
explanation: Scores a word in a document by how often it appears there (TF) times how rare it is across all documents (IDF), so 'the' counts for little and rare topic words count for a lot.
source: Spärck Jones, 'A Statistical Interpretation of Term Specificity and Its Application in Retrieval', Journal of Documentation, 1972 (IDF)

name: Instruction Tuning
explanation: Fine-tune a pre-trained LLM on many tasks phrased as instructions with good answers, so it learns to follow new instructions instead of just continuing text.
source: Wei et al., 'Finetuned Language Models Are Zero-Shot Learners', arXiv 2021 (ICLR 2022; Google)

name: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)
explanation: Aligns an LLM to human preferences with a simple classification-style loss on chosen vs rejected answers, with no separate reward model or RL loop (unlike RLHF).
source: Rafailov et al., 'Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model', NeurIPS, 2023 (Stanford)

name: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)
explanation: A policy gradient method that clips each update so the new policy stays close to the old one. Stable and simple, and the RL algorithm used in classic RLHF.
source: Schulman, Wolski, Dhariwal, Radford & Klimov, 'Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms', arXiv, 2017 (OpenAI)

name: Quantization
explanation: Stores and computes a model's weights (and often activations) with fewer bits, such as 8-bit integers instead of 32-bit floats. Much smaller and faster, with little accuracy loss.
source: Jacob et al., 'Quantization and Training of Neural Networks for Efficient Integer-Arithmetic-Only Inference', CVPR, 2018 (Google)

name: Top-p (Nucleus) Sampling
explanation: When generating text, sample the next token only from the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to p. Avoids both dull and nonsensical text.
source: Holtzman, Buys, Du, Forbes & Choi, 'The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration', arXiv 2019 (ICLR 2020)

name: T5
explanation: An encoder–decoder transformer that treats every NLP task as text in, text out ("translate English to German: …"). Pre-trained by filling in masked spans.
source: Raffel et al., 'Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text Transformer', arXiv 2019 (JMLR 2020; Google)

name: ELMo
explanation: Contextual word embeddings from a bidirectional LSTM language model, so "bank" gets different vectors in "river bank" and "bank account". The step just before BERT.
source: Peters et al., 'Deep Contextualized Word Representations', NAACL, 2018 (Allen Institute for AI & University of Washington)

name: Teacher Forcing
explanation: While training a sequence model, feed it the true previous token instead of its own prediction. Faster, more stable training; transformers train this way too.
source: Williams & Zipser, 'A Learning Algorithm for Continually Running Fully Recurrent Neural Networks', Neural Computation, 1989

name: Backpropagation Through Time
explanation: Trains an RNN by unrolling it over the time steps into one long feed-forward network and running ordinary backpropagation through it.
source: Werbos, 'Backpropagation Through Time: What It Does and How to Do It', Proceedings of the IEEE, 1990

name: Emergent Abilities
explanation: Skills (like multi-step arithmetic) that seem absent in smaller language models and appear once models pass a certain scale. Whether they are truly sudden is debated.
source: Wei et al., 'Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models', Transactions on Machine Learning Research, 2022 (Google)

name: FlashAttention
explanation: Computes exact attention in tiles that fit in the GPU's fast on-chip memory, never storing the full attention matrix. Much faster and lighter, which enabled longer contexts.
source: Dao, Fu, Ermon, Rudra & Ré, 'FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness', NeurIPS, 2022 (Stanford)

name: Speculative Decoding
explanation: A small, fast draft model proposes several tokens, and the big model checks them all in one pass, keeping the ones it agrees with. Same output, faster generation.
source: Leviathan, Kalman & Matias, 'Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding', arXiv 2022 (ICML 2023; Google)

name: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE)
explanation: Encodes position by rotating query and key vectors by an angle that depends on position, so attention scores depend on relative distance. Used in Llama and most modern LLMs.
source: Su et al., 'RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding', arXiv, 2021 (Zhuiyi Technology)

name: Constitutional AI
explanation: Aligns a model using a written list of principles: the AI critiques and revises its own answers, and AI-generated preference labels replace most human ones (RL from AI feedback).
source: Bai et al., 'Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback', arXiv, 2022 (Anthropic)

name: ReAct (LLM Agents)
explanation: An LLM alternates between reasoning in text and taking actions (calling a search engine, a calculator, an API), reading each result before the next step. A basis of LLM agents.
source: Yao et al., 'ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models', arXiv 2022 (ICLR 2023; Princeton & Google)

name: fastText
explanation: Word2Vec extended with character n-grams, so it can build vectors for rare and misspelled words from their pieces. Also a very fast text classifier.
source: Bojanowski, Grave, Joulin & Mikolov, 'Enriching Word Vectors with Subword Information', arXiv 2016 (TACL 2017; Facebook AI Research)

name: Stable Diffusion (Latent Diffusion)
explanation: Runs the diffusion process in the compressed latent space of an autoencoder instead of on pixels, guided by a text encoder. Cheap enough to generate images on a home GPU.
source: Rombach, Blattmann, Lorenz, Esser & Ommer, 'High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models', arXiv 2021 (CVPR 2022; LMU Munich & Runway)

name: Weight Decay
explanation: Shrinks every weight a little at each update, which keeps weights small and reduces overfitting. With plain SGD it is equivalent to an L2 penalty.
source: Krogh & Hertz, 'A Simple Weight Decay Can Improve Generalization', NeurIPS, 1992

name: Learning Rate Schedule
explanation: Changes the learning rate during training, for example warming up, then decaying along a cosine curve. Big steps early, fine steps at the end.
source: Loshchilov & Hutter, 'SGDR: Stochastic Gradient Descent with Warm Restarts', arXiv 2016 (ICLR 2017)

name: AdaGrad
explanation: Gives each parameter its own learning rate that shrinks as its squared gradients add up, so rarely updated features get bigger steps.
source: Duchi, Hazan & Singer, 'Adaptive Subgradient Methods for Online Learning and Stochastic Optimization', JMLR, 2011

name: RMSProp
explanation: Like AdaGrad, but uses a moving average of squared gradients so the step size doesn't shrink forever. Never published as a paper: it comes from a lecture slide.
source: Tieleman & Hinton, Lecture 6.5, 'Neural Networks for Machine Learning', Coursera, 2012

name: Newton's Method
explanation: Uses the second derivative (curvature) as well as the slope to jump straight towards the minimum of a local quadratic approximation. Very fast near the answer, but costly in many dimensions.
source: Raphson, 'Analysis aequationum universalis', 1690 (Newton's earlier version was published by Wallis, 1685)

name: Huber Loss
explanation: Squared error for small mistakes, absolute error for big ones. Fits like least squares but is far less thrown off by outliers.
source: Huber, 'Robust Estimation of a Location Parameter', Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 1964

name: Focal Loss
explanation: Cross-entropy scaled down for examples the model already gets right, so training focuses on the hard ones. Built for object detection, where easy background dominates.
source: Lin, Goyal, Girshick, He & Dollár, 'Focal Loss for Dense Object Detection', ICCV, 2017 (Facebook AI Research)

name: SimCLR
explanation: Learns image features without labels: two random augmentations of the same image should get similar embeddings, and different images different ones (a contrastive loss).
source: Chen, Kornblith, Norouzi & Hinton, 'A Simple Framework for Contrastive Learning of Visual Representations', ICML, 2020 (Google)

name: Leaky ReLU
explanation: ReLU with a small slope for negative inputs instead of zero, so neurons never go completely "dead".
source: Maas, Hannun & Ng, 'Rectifier Nonlinearities Improve Neural Network Acoustic Models', ICML Workshop, 2013

name: GELU
explanation: A smooth ReLU-like activation, x times the normal CDF of x. The usual activation in BERT and GPT-style transformers.
source: Hendrycks & Gimpel, 'Gaussian Error Linear Units (GELUs)', arXiv, 2016

name: Simulated Annealing
explanation: A search that sometimes accepts worse solutions, less often as a 'temperature' cools, so it can escape local minima. Inspired by slowly cooling metal.
source: Kirkpatrick, Gelatt & Vecchi, 'Optimization by Simulated Annealing', Science, 1983 (IBM)

name: Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC)
explanation: Draws samples from a hard probability distribution by running a random walk (a Markov chain) whose long-run behaviour matches it. The workhorse of Bayesian statistics.
source: Metropolis, Rosenbluth, Rosenbluth, Teller & Teller, 'Equation of State Calculations by Fast Computing Machines', Journal of Chemical Physics, 1953

name: Graph Neural Network (GNN)
explanation: A network for graph data: each node repeatedly updates its vector from its neighbours' vectors (message passing). Used for molecules, social networks and maps.
source: Scarselli, Gori, Tsoi, Hagenbuchner & Monfardini, 'The Graph Neural Network Model', IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks, 2009 (GCN: Kipf & Welling, 2016)

name: Siamese Network
explanation: Two copies of the same network embed two inputs, and the distance between the embeddings says whether they match. Used for signatures, faces and similarity search.
source: Bromley, Guyon, LeCun, Säckinger & Shah, 'Signature Verification using a Siamese Time Delay Neural Network', NeurIPS, 1993 (AT&T Bell Labs)

name: Normalizing Flows
explanation: Turns a simple distribution into a complex one through a chain of invertible transformations, so you can both sample and compute exact probabilities.
source: Rezende & Mohamed, 'Variational Inference with Normalizing Flows', ICML, 2015 (DeepMind)

name: StyleGAN
explanation: A GAN that injects a learned 'style' vector at every resolution, giving fine control over features. Famous for photorealistic fake faces.
source: Karras, Laine & Aila, 'A Style-Based Generator Architecture for Generative Adversarial Networks', arXiv 2018 (CVPR 2019; NVIDIA)

name: Gaussian Process
explanation: A distribution over functions: predictions come with uncertainty that grows away from the data. Behind Bayesian optimization.
source: Williams & Rasmussen, 'Gaussian Processes for Regression', NeurIPS, 1996 (geostatistics origins: kriging, 1950s–60s)

name: Generalized Linear Model (GLM)
explanation: Generalizes linear regression with a link function and a non-normal outcome distribution. Logistic and Poisson regression are both GLMs.
source: Nelder & Wedderburn, 'Generalized Linear Models', JRSS A, 1972

name: Quantile Regression
explanation: Predicts a chosen quantile (such as the median or the 90th percentile) instead of the mean. Robust to outliers, and shows how the whole spread changes.
source: Koenker & Bassett, 'Regression Quantiles', Econometrica, 1978

name: Collaborative Filtering
explanation: Recommends items by finding users with similar tastes: 'people who liked what you liked also liked…'. It needs no information about the items themselves.
source: Goldberg, Nichols, Oki & Terry, 'Using Collaborative Filtering to Weave an Information Tapestry', Communications of the ACM, 1992 (Xerox PARC)

name: Matrix Factorization
explanation: Fills in a user × item ratings matrix by learning a small vector for every user and item whose dot products match the known ratings. Made famous by the Netflix Prize.
source: Koren, Bell & Volinsky, 'Matrix Factorization Techniques for Recommender Systems', IEEE Computer, 2009 (Yahoo! Research & AT&T Labs)

name: Stacking
explanation: Trains several different models, then trains a final 'meta' model to combine their predictions. A staple of winning competition entries.
source: Wolpert, 'Stacked Generalization', Neural Networks, 1992

name: Recursive Feature Elimination
explanation: Feature selection by elimination: fit a model, drop the least important feature, refit, and repeat until the desired number of features is left.
source: Guyon, Weston, Barnhill & Vapnik, 'Gene Selection for Cancer Classification using Support Vector Machines', Machine Learning, 2002

name: Bayesian Optimization
explanation: Tunes expensive settings (like hyperparameters) by fitting a probabilistic model, usually a Gaussian process, to past trials and choosing the next trial where improvement looks most likely.
source: Močkus, 'On Bayesian Methods for Seeking the Extremum', Optimization Techniques IFIP Technical Conference, 1975 (popular in ML after Snoek, Larochelle & Adams, 2012)

name: Random Search
explanation: Tries random hyperparameter combinations instead of a full grid. Usually finds good settings faster, because only a few hyperparameters really matter.
source: Bergstra & Bengio, 'Random Search for Hyper-Parameter Optimization', JMLR, 2012

name: Factor Analysis
explanation: Explains correlations between many observed variables with a few hidden factors plus noise. Born in psychology to model "general intelligence".
source: Spearman, "'General Intelligence,' Objectively Determined and Measured", American Journal of Psychology, 1904

name: Independent Component Analysis (ICA)
explanation: Separates mixed signals into statistically independent sources, like isolating each voice from several microphones at a party.
source: Comon, 'Independent Component Analysis, a New Concept?', Signal Processing, 1994

name: Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF)
explanation: Factors a matrix of non-negative values into two non-negative matrices, which gives parts-based components (like topics in documents or parts of faces).
source: Lee & Seung, 'Learning the Parts of Objects by Non-negative Matrix Factorization', Nature, 1999 (Bell Labs)

name: Spectral Clustering
explanation: Builds a similarity graph of the points, embeds them using eigenvectors of the graph's Laplacian, then clusters in that space. Finds non-convex shapes K-means misses.
source: Shi & Malik, 'Normalized Cuts and Image Segmentation', IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence, 2000 (also Ng, Jordan & Weiss, 2001)

name: Mean Shift
explanation: Moves every point uphill towards the densest nearby region until it settles on a peak; points that reach the same peak form a cluster.
source: Fukunaga & Hostetler, 'The Estimation of the Gradient of a Density Function', IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, 1975

name: K-medoids
explanation: Like K-means, but each cluster centre must be an actual data point (a medoid). Works with any distance and resists outliers.
source: Kaufman & Rousseeuw, 'Clustering by Means of Medoids', in Statistical Data Analysis Based on the L1-Norm, 1987

name: Hopfield Network
explanation: A recurrent network that stores patterns as low-energy states and recalls a whole pattern from a partial or noisy one. Part of Hopfield's 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics.
source: Hopfield, 'Neural Networks and Physical Systems with Emergent Collective Computational Abilities', PNAS, 1982

name: Boltzmann Machine
explanation: A stochastic network of binary units that learns a probability distribution over its inputs using an energy function from statistical physics. The restricted version (RBM) powered early deep learning.
source: Ackley, Hinton & Sejnowski, 'A Learning Algorithm for Boltzmann Machines', Cognitive Science, 1985

name: Deep Belief Network
explanation: A stack of RBMs trained one layer at a time without labels, then fine-tuned. In 2006 it showed deep networks could be trained, which helped restart deep learning.
source: Hinton, Osindero & Teh, 'A Fast Learning Algorithm for Deep Belief Nets', Neural Computation, 2006

name: AlphaGo
explanation: Combined deep policy and value networks with Monte Carlo tree search, trained on expert games and self-play. In 2016 it beat Lee Sedol, one of the best Go players in the world.
source: Silver et al., 'Mastering the Game of Go with Deep Neural Networks and Tree Search', Nature, 2016 (DeepMind)

name: Monte Carlo Tree Search
explanation: Plans by repeatedly simulating random play-outs from the current position and growing a search tree towards the most promising moves.
source: Kocsis & Szepesvári, 'Bandit Based Monte-Carlo Planning', ECML, 2006 (also Coulom, 2006)

name: Temporal Difference Learning
explanation: Updates a value estimate toward the reward plus the next state's estimate, learning from each step instead of waiting for the episode to end. Q-learning is a TD method.
source: Sutton, 'Learning to Predict by the Methods of Temporal Differences', Machine Learning, 1988

name: Actor-Critic
explanation: Two parts learn together: the actor (policy) chooses actions, and the critic (value function) judges them. The critic's feedback lowers the noise of policy gradients.
source: Barto, Sutton & Anderson, 'Neuronlike Adaptive Elements That Can Solve Difficult Learning Control Problems', IEEE Transactions on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics, 1983

name: Epsilon-greedy
explanation: The simplest exploration rule: with probability ε take a random action, otherwise take the best known one.
source: Watkins, 'Learning from Delayed Rewards', PhD thesis, University of Cambridge, 1989

name: Inverse Reinforcement Learning
explanation: Works backwards from an expert's behaviour to the reward function they seem to be optimizing, then learns a policy from it.
source: Ng & Russell, 'Algorithms for Inverse Reinforcement Learning', ICML, 2000

name: Probit Model
explanation: Like logistic regression, but squashes the linear score with the normal distribution's CDF instead of the sigmoid. Common in economics.
source: Bliss, 'The Method of Probits', Science, 1934

name: LOWESS
explanation: Draws a smooth curve through a scatter plot by fitting many small weighted regressions, each centred on one point and using only its neighbours.
source: Cleveland, 'Robust Locally Weighted Regression and Smoothing Scatterplots', JASA, 1979

name: Spline
explanation: A curve made of polynomial pieces joined smoothly at knots. Splines let regression models bend to fit non-linear trends.
source: Schoenberg, 'Contributions to the Problem of Approximation of Equidistant Data by Analytic Functions', Quarterly of Applied Mathematics, 1946

name: Cox Proportional Hazards
explanation: Models how features change the risk (hazard) of an event over time, like death or customer churn, without assuming the shape of the baseline risk.
source: Cox, 'Regression Models and Life-Tables', JRSS B, 1972

name: Kalman Filter
explanation: Tracks a hidden state over time (like a vehicle's position) by alternating a prediction from a motion model with a correction from noisy measurements. Used in the Apollo guidance computer.
source: Kalman, 'A New Approach to Linear Filtering and Prediction Problems', Journal of Basic Engineering, 1960

name: Brier Score
explanation: The mean squared difference between predicted probabilities and what actually happened (0 or 1). Rewards forecasts that are both accurate and well calibrated.
source: Brier, 'Verification of Forecasts Expressed in Terms of Probability', Monthly Weather Review, 1950

name: Matthews Correlation Coefficient
explanation: A correlation between predicted and actual binary labels, using all four cells of the confusion matrix. Stays honest on heavily imbalanced data.
source: Matthews, 'Comparison of the Predicted and Observed Secondary Structure of T4 Phage Lysozyme', Biochimica et Biophysica Acta, 1975

name: Cohen's Kappa
explanation: Agreement between two labellers (or a model and the truth), corrected for the agreement you would expect by chance.
source: Cohen, 'A Coefficient of Agreement for Nominal Scales', Educational and Psychological Measurement, 1960

name: Chi-squared Test
explanation: Tests whether observed counts differ from expected counts by more than chance, for example whether two categorical variables are independent.
source: Karl Pearson, 'On the Criterion that a Given System of Deviations from the Probable…', Philosophical Magazine, 1900

name: Mann–Whitney U Test
explanation: Compares two groups using ranks instead of raw values, so it doesn't assume normal data. Its U statistic is closely tied to AUC.
source: Mann & Whitney, 'On a Test of Whether One of Two Random Variables is Stochastically Larger than the Other', Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 1947

name: Confidence Interval
explanation: A range built so that, across repeated experiments, it would contain the true value a set share of the time (such as 95%). It shows how uncertain an estimate is.
source: Neyman, 'Outline of a Theory of Statistical Estimation Based on the Classical Theory of Probability', Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A, 1937

name: Null Hypothesis
explanation: The default assumption of 'no effect' that a statistical test tries to reject. Rejecting it means the data would be surprising if there really were no effect.
source: Fisher, 'The Design of Experiments', 1935 (coined the term)

name: False Discovery Rate
explanation: When running many tests at once, controls the expected share of false positives among the results you call significant, instead of the chance of any false positive at all.
source: Benjamini & Hochberg, 'Controlling the False Discovery Rate: A Practical and Powerful Approach to Multiple Testing', JRSS B, 1995

name: Standard Deviation
explanation: The typical distance of values from their mean: the square root of the variance, in the same units as the data.
source: Karl Pearson, 'Contributions to the Mathematical Theory of Evolution', Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A, 1894 (coined the term)

name: Variance
explanation: The average squared distance of values from their mean. It measures spread and is the basis of ANOVA, PCA and the bias–variance tradeoff.
source: Fisher, 'The Correlation between Relatives on the Supposition of Mendelian Inheritance', Transactions of the Royal Society of Edinburgh, 1918 (coined the term)

name: Matrix Multiplication
explanation: Combines two matrices by taking dot products of the first's rows with the second's columns. Neural networks are mostly matrix multiplications, which is why GPUs matter.
source: Cayley, 'A Memoir on the Theory of Matrices', Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London, 1858

name: Law of Large Numbers
explanation: As you take more samples, their average gets closer and closer to the true expected value. Why more data gives more reliable estimates.
source: Jacob Bernoulli, 'Ars Conjectandi', 1713 (published posthumously)

name: Simpson's Paradox
explanation: A trend that appears in every subgroup can reverse when the groups are combined, because of a hidden confounding variable.
source: Simpson, 'The Interpretation of Interaction in Contingency Tables', JRSS B, 1951 (noted earlier by Yule, 1903)

name: Spearman Correlation
explanation: Pearson correlation computed on ranks instead of raw values, so it measures any monotonic relationship, not just straight lines, and shrugs off outliers.
source: Spearman, 'The Proof and Measurement of Association between Two Things', American Journal of Psychology, 1904

name: Fourier Transform
explanation: Rewrites a signal as a sum of sine waves of different frequencies. Basic to audio and signal processing, and it inspired sinusoidal positional encodings.
source: Fourier, 'Théorie analytique de la chaleur', 1822

name: pandas
explanation: The Python library for tables (DataFrames): load, clean, filter, group and join data. Usually the first step of any ML project.
source: Started by Wes McKinney at AQR Capital in 2008 (open-sourced 2009); McKinney, 'Data Structures for Statistical Computing in Python', SciPy, 2010

name: Matplotlib
explanation: Python's classic plotting library: line plots, scatter plots, histograms and more. Most other Python plotting tools are built on it.
source: First released by John D. Hunter, 2003; Hunter, 'Matplotlib: A 2D Graphics Environment', Computing in Science & Engineering, 2007

name: Jupyter Notebook
explanation: Interactive documents that mix live code, results, plots and text in cells. The default place where data scientists explore and teach.
source: Project Jupyter spun off from IPython in 2014 (IPython Notebook 2011; IPython by Fernando Pérez, 2001)

name: Hugging Face Transformers
explanation: The open-source library (and model hub) that lets you download and run thousands of pre-trained transformers in a few lines of Python.
source: Wolf et al., 'HuggingFace's Transformers: State-of-the-art Natural Language Processing', arXiv, 2019 (Hugging Face)

name: JAX
explanation: Google's library for NumPy-style code with automatic differentiation and XLA compilation to GPUs and TPUs, built from composable transforms (grad, jit, vmap).
source: Bradbury et al., 'JAX: Composable Transformations of Python+NumPy Programs', 2018 (Google)

name: CUDA
explanation: NVIDIA's platform for running general-purpose code on GPUs. Deep learning frameworks rely on it for fast matrix multiplication.
source: First released by NVIDIA, February 2007

name: LangChain
explanation: A framework for building LLM applications by chaining prompts, models, retrievers and tools, often used for RAG and agents.
source: First released by Harrison Chase, October 2022 (now developed by LangChain, Inc.)

name: R (programming language)
explanation: A programming language built for statistics and data analysis, with thousands of packages on CRAN. StatQuest has many R tutorials.
source: Created by Ross Ihaka & Robert Gentleman, first announced 1993; Ihaka & Gentleman, 'R: A Language for Data Analysis and Graphics', JCGS, 1996

name: Turing Test
explanation: Turing's 'imitation game': if a judge chatting by text can't reliably tell a machine from a human, the machine passes.
source: Turing, 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence', Mind, 1950

name: Artificial Intelligence
explanation: The field of making machines do things that would need intelligence if people did them. The name was coined for the 1956 Dartmouth workshop.
source: McCarthy, Minsky, Rochester & Shannon, 'A Proposal for the Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence', 1955

name: Machine Learning
explanation: Getting computers to improve at a task from data or experience instead of being explicitly programmed. Samuel coined the term with a checkers program that learned to beat him.
source: Samuel, 'Some Studies in Machine Learning Using the Game of Checkers', IBM Journal of Research and Development, 1959
